name: Umeda
confidence_why: No phonological description of Umeda exists: the only remark on stress anywhere is Gell 1975's aside that Umedas say 'umda, 'puda, sa'wada, 'waina and wa'yala, five village names all stressed on the penultimate syllable, which hints at penultimate stress but is no rule, and Seiler 1984 and 1985 say nothing about Punda stress.

The dialects spoken to the south, in the Amanab sub-district are not intelligible to Umeda speakers — (I shall call the Umeda-Punda dialect ‘Umeda’ henceforth). […] Umedas pronounce the name of their village 'umda (with the stress falling on the first syllable) and the names of the other villages '‘puda, sa'wada, 'waina, wa'yala.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated. Gell (an anthropologist, self-described as linguistically naive) marks stress only on five village names: 'umda, 'puda, 'waina (initial = penultimate in disyllables) and sa'wada, wa'yala (second = penultimate in trisyllables). All five are consistent with penultimate stress and inconsistent with fixed initial stress; this is an inference from five proper names, not a description of the stress system.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the remark concerns village names only. Note the closest described relative, Imonda (Seiler 1985: 10), is said to have no contrastive stress, 'stress being approximately equal on all syllables'.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated proper names (village names) in citation form; nothing on phrase-level prosody, and no general word-stress claim.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog umed1238 'Umeda-Punda' [upi] = Seiler's (1985) 'Punda' (the language of the villages Umeda and Punda, split by Seiler from Laycock's 'Waina-Sowanda') = Gell's (1975) 'Umeda' (his 'Umeda-Punda dialect', which he treats as mutually intelligible with the Waina-Wyalla/Sowanda dialect, i.e. Sowanda [sow]). Gell's stress remark concerns Umeda village speech.
